name: Sample space
quick: The outcomes distinguished by a model.
definition: The set $\Omega$ of possible outcomes of a specified experiment.
example: Two ordered binary reports give $\{PP,PF,FP,FF\}$.
confusion: A coarser recording rule can merge outcomes with unequal total probabilities.
section: Specify the experiment before calculating

name: Event
quick: A set of outcomes.
definition: A subset $A\subseteq\Omega$; it occurs when the observed outcome lies in $A$.
example: Exactly one failure is $\{PF,FP\}$.
confusion: An event may contain several outcomes.
section: Specify the experiment before calculating

name: Disjoint events
quick: Events with no common outcome.
example: A single die roll cannot equal both $1$ and $2$.
confusion: Disjoint does not mean independent.
section: Translate event language into sets

name: Complement
quick: All outcomes outside the event.
example: The complement of at least one failure is no failures.
confusion: The complement of both is not both, not neither.
section: Translate event language into sets

name: Probability model
quick: Outcomes together with consistent probability assignments.
definition: A sample space and event probabilities satisfying nonnegativity, normalization, and countable additivity.
example: Four outcomes may have weights $0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4$.
confusion: A list of possibilities does not supply their probabilities.
section: Probability weights and the axioms

name: Equally likely outcomes
quick: Outcomes assigned the same probability.
definition: In a finite space of size $N$, equal singleton weights are $1/N$.
example: A fair eight-sided die gives each face probability $1/8$.
confusion: Equal labels or an unknown bias do not justify equal weights.
section: Probability weights and the axioms

name: Inclusion-exclusion
quick: Add individual probabilities and correct for overlap.
confusion: Subtract the intersection once, because it was counted twice.
section: Complements, overlap, and bounds

name: Union bound
quick: An upper bound that needs no independence.
example: Three failure probabilities $0.01$ give an any-failure bound $0.03$.
confusion: The sum need not equal the union probability.
section: Complements, overlap, and bounds

name: Partition
quick: Disjoint pieces covering the whole space.
definition: Events $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint and satisfy $\bigcup_iB_i=\Omega$.
example: Both, only $A$, only $B$, and neither form a partition.
confusion: Coverage alone is insufficient if the pieces overlap.
section: Build and audit a complete event model

name: Multiplication principle
quick: Count successive choices by multiplying their counts.
definition: With $n_i$ choices at stage $i$ for each prior history, the number of complete outcomes is $\prod_i n_i$.
example: Four shapes and three colors give $12$ badges.
confusion: Varying branch counts must be handled separately.
section: Count stages and identify the sampling rule

name: Sampling with replacement
quick: Selected items remain available for later draws.
definition: After selection the item returns to the pool, so repetition is possible.
example: Two draws from three labels have $3^2$ ordered outcomes.
confusion: Replacement alone does not imply uniform or independent draws.
section: Count stages and identify the sampling rule

name: Ordered selection
quick: A list of distinct selected objects.
definition: The count of length-$k$ ordered selections is $(n)_k=n!/(n-k)!$.
example: Three named roles among seven people give $210$ assignments.
confusion: Named roles retain order; a committee does not.
section: Ordered selections and factorials

name: Factorial
quick: The product of the positive integers through $n$.
confusion: Factorials count arrangements of distinct labeled objects before any symmetry correction.
section: Ordered selections and factorials

name: Combination
quick: An unordered selection of distinct objects.
definition: There are $\binom nk=n!/[k!(n-k)!]$ subsets of size $k$ from $n$ objects.
confusion: A combination does not distinguish role assignments among the selected objects.
section: Unordered selections and combinations

name: Binomial coefficient
quick: A subset count and expansion coefficient.
definition: $\binom nk$ counts choices of $k$ positions and multiplies $a^kb^{n-k}$ in $(a+b)^n$.
example: $\binom62=15$ counts six-bit strings with two ones.
confusion: It counts arrangements of success positions, not their probabilities.
section: Unordered selections and combinations

name: Uniform subset sample
quick: Every subset of the specified size has the same probability.
definition: A size-$k$ sample from $n$ objects assigns probability $1/\binom nk$ to each subset.
example: A pair from seven tokens has $21$ equally likely possibilities.
confusion: Uniform categories need not produce uniform objects.
section: Use compatible numerator and denominator counts

name: Collision
quick: Two or more selections share a value.
definition: For independent uniform labels, a collision is the complement of all labels being distinct.
example: Three labels from five collide with probability $13/25$.
confusion: Any matching pair is a larger event than a match with one designated selection.
section: Complements, collisions, and counting arguments

name: Conditional probability
quick: Probability after restricting to given information.
example: Ten matching records among sixteen retained records give $5/8$.
confusion: The denominator refers to the event after the bar.
section: Conditioning changes the reference population

name: Joint event probability
quick: The probability that several events all occur.
definition: For two events it is $P(A\cap B)$.
example: Ten matching records among forty give joint probability $1/4$.
confusion: A joint probability does not renormalize to a subgroup.
section: Conditioning changes the reference population

name: Probability multiplication rule
quick: Recover joint probability from a conditional probability.
example: Red then blue without replacement gives $(4/6)(2/5)$.
confusion: The second factor is conditional unless independence is justified.
section: Read tables and multiply along a history

name: Probability tree
quick: A diagram of conditional branches through successive stages.
definition: Path probabilities multiply conditional branch probabilities; disjoint path probabilities add.
example: The red-blue and blue-red paths both contribute to one of each color.
confusion: Outgoing probabilities sum to one at each reachable node, not across unrelated nodes.
section: Read tables and multiply along a history

name: Independent events
quick: Events whose joint probability factors.
example: Two events of probabilities $1/2$ with overlap $1/4$ are independent.
confusion: Disjoint positive-probability events are dependent, not independent.
section: Independence is a testable factorization

name: Mutual independence
quick: Every subcollection has a factored intersection probability.
definition: For each nonempty index set $I$, $P(\bigcap_{i\in I}A_i)=\prod_{i\in I}P(A_i)$.
example: Independent trial outcomes satisfy the product rule for any selected trials.
confusion: Pairwise independence checks fewer equations.
section: Repeated trials and mutual independence

name: Pairwise independence
quick: Every pair of distinct events is independent.
example: Two fair bits and their agreement event form a pairwise-independent example.
confusion: Three-way or larger intersections may still fail factorization.
section: Repeated trials and mutual independence

name: Conditional independence of events
quick: Independence inside a specified information set.
example: A shared setting can be included in $C$ before testing factorization.
confusion: Unconditional independence can fail after selection, and the converse can fail too.
section: Conditioning, selection, and causal restraint

name: Law of total probability
quick: Average conditional probabilities across a partition.
example: Server timeout rates $0.02,0.08$ with weights $0.7,0.3$ yield $0.038$.
confusion: Conditional rates must be multiplied by the probabilities of their cases.
section: Total probability is a weighted average

name: Prior probability
quick: A case probability before the specified new evidence.
example: A source selected with probability $0.3$ has prior $0.3$.
confusion: Prior means before this evidence, not necessarily before all knowledge.
section: Reverse the question with Bayes rule

name: Likelihood of evidence
quick: Probability of the observed evidence under a case.
definition: For observed event $E$, the likelihood under $B_i$ is $P(E\mid B_i)$.
example: A timeout rate $0.08$ is the timeout likelihood under its server.
confusion: Likelihoods over cases need not sum to one.
section: Reverse the question with Bayes rule

name: Posterior probability
quick: A case probability after conditioning on evidence.
example: The timeout example gives posterior $12/19$ for server $V$.
confusion: Reverse conditioning requires the prior and the normalization denominator.
section: Reverse the question with Bayes rule

name: Base rate
quick: The overall prevalence of a category before the signal.
definition: The prior $P(D)$ in a screening model.
example: Two percent defective means base rate $0.02$.
confusion: Signal accuracy alone does not determine the posterior.
section: Base rates and screening tables

name: Sensitivity
quick: Positive-signal probability within the target category.
example: Flagging $90\%$ of defective items gives sensitivity $0.9$.
confusion: It is not the probability an item is defective given a flag.
section: Base rates and screening tables

name: Specificity
quick: Negative-signal probability outside the target category.
example: False-positive rate $0.05$ corresponds to specificity $0.95$.
confusion: Specificity complements the false-positive rate, not sensitivity.
section: Base rates and screening tables

name: Odds
quick: Probability divided by its complementary probability.
example: Probability $3/4$ gives odds $3:1$.
confusion: Odds and probability use different scales.
section: Odds and sequential evidence

name: Likelihood ratio
quick: Relative compatibility of evidence under two cases.
definition: $P(E\mid H)/P(E\mid H^c)$ when the denominator is positive.
example: A ratio of six multiplies prior odds by six.
confusion: Repeated evidence ratios multiply only with the appropriate conditional likelihoods.
section: Odds and sequential evidence

name: Finite mixture model
quick: A probability model formed by weighting component models.
definition: $P(E)=\sum_iP(E\mid B_i)P(B_i)$ with a latent or observed partition label.
example: A hidden high-success or low-success environment determines conditional trial rates.
confusion: Independence within each component need not survive mixing.
section: Compare mechanisms and audit an update

name: Random variable
quick: A numerical function of an uncertain outcome.
example: A failure count maps $PFP$ to $1$.
confusion: The random variable is a function; its realized value is a number.
section: A random variable records a numerical feature

name: Discrete support
quick: Values with positive probability mass.
definition: The set $\{x:P(X=x)>0\}$ for a discrete distribution.
example: A count of two fair heads has support $\{0,1,2\}$.
confusion: Discrete values need not be integers or equally likely.
section: A random variable records a numerical feature

name: Probability mass function
quick: The probability assigned to each discrete value.
confusion: Mass is probability at a value, not cumulative probability through it.
section: Construct and check a probability mass function

name: Cumulative distribution function
quick: Probability at or below a threshold.
confusion: The equality at the threshold includes its probability mass.
section: Accumulate mass into a CDF

name: CDF jump
quick: The point mass added at a value.
example: A jump from $1/4$ to $3/4$ adds mass $1/2$.
confusion: A cumulative level itself is not the point mass.
section: Accumulate mass into a CDF

name: Tail probability
quick: Probability beyond a specified threshold.
example: For integer $X$, $P(X\geq3)=1-F_X(2)$.
confusion: Strict and inclusive tails differ by the mass at the threshold.
section: Intervals, tails, and endpoint discipline

name: Transformed random variable
quick: A new numerical feature obtained by applying a function.
example: Squaring merges masses at $-2$ and $2$ into mass at $4$.
confusion: Transform values first; do not apply the value transformation to their probabilities.
section: Transform values and combine their masses

name: Expectation
quick: The probability-weighted mean of a variable.
example: Counts $0,1,3$ with masses $0.5,0.3,0.2$ have mean $0.9$.
confusion: The mean need not be a possible or most likely outcome.
section: Expectation is a probability-weighted mean

name: Integrable random variable
quick: A variable with finite expected absolute value.
example: Every finite-support real-valued variable is integrable.
confusion: A valid infinite-support PMF need not have a finite mean.
section: Expectation is a probability-weighted mean

name: Linearity of expectation
quick: Expectations distribute over finite linear combinations.
example: $E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]$ even when the variables are dependent.
confusion: Linearity does not extend to arbitrary nonlinear functions.
section: Transformations, linearity, and indicators

name: Indicator variable
quick: A zero-one variable recording whether an event occurs.
example: A count can be the sum of indicators for its contributing events.
confusion: Indicator expectations add without independence.
section: Transformations, linearity, and indicators

name: Variance
quick: Expected squared deviation from the mean.
example: Equal masses at one and five have variance four.
confusion: Variance has squared units and is not linear.
section: Variance and standard deviation measure spread

name: Standard deviation
quick: The nonnegative square root of variance.
example: Variance four square minutes gives standard deviation two minutes.
confusion: It is not the expected absolute deviation.
section: Variance and standard deviation measure spread

name: Variance scaling
quick: Squared scaling changes variance; translation does not.
example: Tripling a variable multiplies its variance by nine.
confusion: The scale factor for standard deviation is $|a|$, not $a^2$.
section: Scaling, sums, and the role of dependence

name: Second moment
quick: The expected square of a variable.
example: It equals variance plus the squared mean.
confusion: The second moment is not the square of the expectation.
section: Use moments without losing the full model

name: Bernoulli distribution
quick: A zero-one distribution with one success probability.
example: A timeout indicator may be $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.03)$.
confusion: Success is a coding convention, not necessarily a desirable outcome.
section: Bernoulli variables model one binary event

name: Binomial distribution
quick: The success count in a fixed number of independent equal-rate trials.
example: Five independent trials with $p=1/3$ give $P(X=2)=80/243$.
confusion: Fixed trial count, common probability, and independence are separate assumptions.
section: Binomial counts combine fixed independent trials

name: Binomial sample proportion
quick: A binomial count divided by its positive trial count.
definition: For $X\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$ and $n>0$, $\widehat p=X/n$ has mean $p$ and variance $p(1-p)/n$.
example: A count of three in ten trials gives observed proportion $0.3$.
confusion: An observed proportion is not automatically the model parameter.
section: Binomial tails and model checks

name: Geometric distribution
quick: The trial number of the first success.
confusion: Some sources count failures instead, shifting the variable down by one.
section: Geometric waiting time counts through first success

name: Geometric memorylessness
quick: Previous failures do not change the remaining waiting-time distribution.
example: After five failures, the next trial still succeeds with probability $p$.
confusion: It requires the constant-rate independent model and does not describe learning or depletion.
section: Geometric moments and memorylessness

name: Hypergeometric distribution
quick: A marked count in a uniform sample without replacement.
confusion: This subject orders parameters as population size, marked count, sample size.
section: Hypergeometric counts sample without replacement

name: Finite-population correction
quick: The variance reduction caused by sampling without replacement.
definition: For a hypergeometric count and $N>1$, multiply $np(1-p)$ by $(N-n)/(N-1)$.
example: Sampling all $N$ objects makes the correction zero.
confusion: It changes the variance, not the expected count $np$.
section: Finite populations reduce count variance

name: Poisson distribution
quick: A nonnegative count distribution with equal mean and variance.
example: With mean two, $P(X=0)=e^{-2}$.
confusion: The parameter belongs to a specified interval; it is not a success probability.
section: Poisson counts have an interval-specific mean

name: Poisson exposure parameter
quick: Rate multiplied by the size of the observation interval.
definition: For rate $r$ and exposure $t$, the count mean is $\lambda=rt$.
example: Six arrivals per hour over twenty minutes gives $\lambda=2$.
confusion: Convert units before multiplying; rate and interval mean are different quantities.
section: Rates, exposure, and independent counts

name: Poisson approximation to a binomial count
aliases: Poisson approximation to a binomial count
quick: A rare-success approximation preserving the mean.
definition: Approximate $\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)$ by $\operatorname{Poisson}(np)$ when the setting and required accuracy justify it.
example: For $n=100,p=0.01$, no success is approximately $e^{-1}$.
confusion: The approximation is not an exact distributional identity or a universal tail-accuracy guarantee.
section: Approximation and choosing a model

name: Probability density
quick: Probability per unit of the variable.
definition: A nonnegative function integrating to one whose integral over a region gives its probability.
example: $f(x)=3x^2$ on $(0,1)$ integrates to one.
confusion: A density height may exceed one; an event probability may not.
section: Probability is area, not height

name: Continuous CDF
quick: Accumulated probability up to a location.
example: Density $3x^2$ on $(0,1)$ gives $F(x)=x^3$ there.
confusion: The CDF is an area, not the density height.
section: Move between density and cumulative probability

name: Quantile
quick: A location corresponding to a cumulative probability.
definition: For a strictly increasing continuous CDF, $F(q_p)=p$.
example: A uniform $(0,8)$ variable has $q_{0.75}=6$.
confusion: A percentile level and its quantile have different units.
section: Move between density and cumulative probability

name: Integral expectation
quick: An average weighted by density.
example: With density $4x^3$ on $(0,1)$, $E[X]=4/5$.
confusion:
Usually $E[g(X)]
e g(E[X])$.
section: Compute expectations by integration

name: Continuous uniform distribution
quick: Equal-length intervals have equal probabilities within the support.
example: For $X\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(2,8)$, $E[X]=5$.
confusion: A bounded range alone does not justify uniformity.
section: Uniform models and interval conditioning

name: Exponential rate
quick: The reciprocal of the mean exponential waiting time.
example: Rate $1/4$ per minute gives mean four minutes.
confusion: Rate and mean parameterizations are reciprocals.
section: Exponential waiting times and their limitations

name: Exponential memorylessness
quick: The remaining wait has the original distribution.
example: An extra two-minute wait has probability $e^{-2\lambda}$ even after waiting five minutes.
confusion: The property depends on the model; past waiting is not universally irrelevant.
section: Exponential waiting times and their limitations

name: Normal distribution
quick: A symmetric continuous distribution specified by mean and variance.
example: $N(30,16)$ has standard deviation four.
confusion: The second argument here is variance, not standard deviation.
section: Normal models have a location and a scale

name: Standardization
quick: Center a variable and measure it in standard-deviation units.
definition: $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$ for finite mean and positive finite standard deviation.
example: $38$ has score $2$ under $N(30,16)$.
confusion: Standardizing does not by itself produce normality.
section: Normal models have a location and a scale

name: Standard normal CDF
quick: $\Phi(z)$ is the standard normal left-tail probability.
confusion: A right-tail probability is $1-Phi(z)$.
section: Use the normal CDF without confusing tails

name: Normal quantile
quick: A normal threshold with a specified probability below it.
confusion: A central 95% interval uses the 97.5% quantile at its upper end.
section: Quantiles and affine changes of units

name: Density transformation
quick: Adjust a density for the change of coordinate width.
definition: For a differentiable monotone inverse $h$, $f_Y(y)=f_X(h(y))|h'(y)|$ on the transformed support.
example: For $U\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(1,3)$, $1/U$ has density $1/(2y^2)$ on $(1/3,1)$.
confusion: Substitution alone misses the derivative factor.
section: Transform a distribution through its CDF

name: Point mass created by a transformation
aliases: Point mass created by a transformation
quick: A positive-probability set can be collapsed to one output.
definition: If $P(g(X)=c)>0$, the transformed CDF jumps at $c$.
example: Clipping a uniform $(-1,1)$ variable below at zero gives $P(Y=0)=1/2$.
confusion: An infinite density height is different from a positive point mass.
section: Account for branches and point masses

name: Joint PMF
quick: Probabilities of simultaneous values of discrete variables.
definition: $p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y)$, with all cell probabilities summing to one.
example: For fair independent bits, each of the four pairs has probability $1/4$.
confusion: Marginal probabilities alone do not specify the joint PMF.
section: A joint table retains how variables occur together

name: Marginal distribution
quick: The distribution of one coordinate after summing or integrating out the other.
example: A row sum gives $P(X=x)$ when rows index $X$.
confusion: Marginalizing is not conditioning on a particular value.
section: A joint table retains how variables occur together

name: Conditional PMF
quick: A discrete distribution within a specified positive-probability condition.
example: A row of joint probabilities is normalized by its row total.
confusion: A joint table row usually sums to less than one; its conditional version sums to one.
section: Condition a table and test independence

name: Joint density
quick: Probability per unit area in a pair of continuous coordinates.
example: Density $2$ on $0<x<y<1$ integrates to one.
confusion: A constant density over a nonrectangular region need not make its coordinates independent.
section: A joint density assigns probability to regions

name: Conditional density
quick: A density for one variable when another is specified.
example: Under density $2$ on $0<x<y<1$, $Y\mid X=x$ is uniform on $(x,1)$.
confusion: The denominator is a density, not the zero point probability $P(X=x)$.
section: Condition continuous variables using densities

name: Joint CDF
quick: Probability that both coordinates lie below their thresholds.
example: For independent uniform coordinates on $(0,1)$, $F(x,y)=xy$ inside the square.
confusion: Rectangle probabilities need four CDF terms, not just two.
section: Check the whole joint model

name: Covariance
quick: The expected product of centered deviations.
example: For fair bits with joint success probability $3/8$, covariance is $1/8$.
confusion: Zero covariance does not generally establish independence.
section: Covariance measures centered co-variation

name: Variance of a linear combination
quick: Variance includes both squared coefficients and covariance terms.
example: Variances four and nine with covariance three give sum variance nineteen.
confusion: A minus sign on $Y$ changes the cross term, not $operatorname{Var}(Y)$.
section: Variance of a combination includes cross terms

name: Correlation coefficient
quick: Covariance normalized by the two standard deviations.
example: Covariance three with standard deviations two and three gives correlation $1/2$.
confusion: Correlation is undefined for a constant variable; zero correlation does not ensure independence.
section: Correlation standardizes covariance but does not describe all dependence

name: Covariance matrix
quick: The matrix of all pairwise component covariances.
example: Diagonal entries are variances; off-diagonal entries describe co-variation.
confusion: A covariance matrix is not generally the matrix $E[mathbf Xmathbf X^T]$ unless the mean is zero.
section: Collect means and covariances into vectors and matrices

name: Positive semidefinite covariance
quick: Every linear projection has nonnegative variance.
definition: $\mathbf a^T\Sigma\mathbf a\ge0$ for every real vector $\mathbf a$.
example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ is valid but singular.
confusion: Positive diagonal entries alone are insufficient for covariance validity.
section: Covariance geometry, validity, and redundant features

name: Conditional expectation
quick: An average under a conditional distribution.
example: If $Y\mid X=x$ is uniform on $(x,1)$, its mean is $(x+1)/2$.
confusion: The conditional expectation given a random variable is itself a random variable.
section: A conditional mean is a function of the information

name: Law of total expectation
quick: Average conditional means using the probabilities of the conditions.
example: Group means one and four with weights $3/4,1/4$ give mean $7/4$.
confusion: Do not average group means equally unless their population weights are equal.
section: Average conditional means to recover the overall mean

name: Law of total variance
quick: Total variation equals average conditional variation plus variation of conditional means.
example: Within variation three and between variation $27/4$ give total $39/4$.
confusion: Conditional variance decreases on average, not necessarily for every observed condition.
section: Split variation within and between conditions

name: Conditional mean prediction
quick: The best prediction under expected squared-error loss.
example: For conditional mean four and variance nine, predicting six has MSE thirteen.
confusion: Optimality depends on the loss; the mean is not automatically optimal for every prediction objective.
section: Conditional means give optimal squared-error predictions

name: Random sum moments
quick: Separate randomness in count from randomness in each contribution.
definition: For iid contributions independent of $N$, $E[S]=\mu E[N]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(S)=vE[N]+\mu^2\operatorname{Var}(N)$.
example: Count moments five and two, contribution moments three and four, give total mean fifteen and variance thirty-eight.
confusion: A data-dependent stopping count need not satisfy the independence assumption.
section: Use conditioning to analyze random workloads

name: Parameter and statistic
quick: A parameter describes the target population; a statistic describes the sample.
definition: The population mean is $\mu$; the observed sample mean is $\bar x$.
example: The failure proportion in all requests is a parameter; the proportion in a sampled batch is a statistic.
confusion: A statistic becomes a known value after observation, though its sampling version is random.
section: Define the population, observation, and question

name: Observational unit
quick: The entity on which variables are measured.
definition: A unit may be a person, device, request, experiment, or other defined entity.
example: Repeated readings from one device do not create new devices.
confusion: Rows, measurements, and independent units are not automatically the same thing.
section: Define the population, observation, and question

name: Sample mean and median
quick: Two distinct summaries of numerical location.
definition: $\bar x=\sum_i x_i/n$; the median is the middle ordered value, averaging the two middle values when $n$ is even.
example: Data $1,2,2,3,12$ have mean four and median two.
confusion: The mean and median need not agree, especially with skew or extreme values.
section: Summarize location without hiding the data

name: Sample variance
quick: Squared sample spread computed with denominator n minus one.
confusion: The empirical-distribution variance uses denominator $n$, a different convention.
section: Describe spread and distinguish empirical from model variation

name: Sampling design
quick: The rule determining which population units are observed.
definition: A probability sampling design uses specified random selection, such as simple random, stratified, or cluster sampling.
example: Stratification samples within groups; cluster sampling selects groups.
confusion: A large convenience sample does not become a probability sample merely by growing.
section: Connect the sampling design to the target population

name: Sampling frame
quick: The accessible list or collection used to select units.
definition: Coverage of the target population depends on what the frame includes and excludes.
example: An active-user list omits users who stopped using the service.
confusion: Random selection within a frame does not repair missing coverage.
section: Connect the sampling design to the target population

name: Random assignment
quick: Use a chance process to assign treatments to study units.
definition: Assignment supports treatment comparisons by making pretreatment factors comparable in distribution.
example: Randomly assigning interface versions differs from observing user-selected versions.
confusion: Random assignment does not guarantee exact finite-sample balance or representative sampling.
section: Separate random error, systematic bias, and causal evidence

name: Selection bias
quick: Systematic distortion caused by which observations enter the data.
definition: Selection related to relevant outcomes can make the observed sample differ from the target population.
example: Dropping unrecorded timeouts can underrepresent long request durations.
confusion: More observations from the same biased mechanism need not fix the distortion.
section: Separate random error, systematic bias, and causal evidence

name: Sampling distribution
quick: The probability distribution of a statistic under repeated sampling.
definition: For iid observations, $\bar X_n$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2/n$.
example: The mean of two independent fair bits takes $0,1/2,1$.
confusion: The sampling distribution of means differs from the distribution of individual observations.
section: A statistic has a sampling distribution

name: Standard error of the mean
quick: The standard deviation of the sample mean.
definition: For iid observations of variance $\sigma^2$, $\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n)=\sigma/\sqrt n$.
example: Population standard deviation twelve and sample size thirty-six give standard error two.
confusion: Standard error is not the standard deviation of individual observations.
section: A statistic has a sampling distribution

name: Weak law of large numbers
quick: A fixed error in an iid average becomes unlikely as sample size grows.
definition: For integrable iid observations, $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.
example: For finite variance the error probability is at most $\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$.
confusion: The result does not guarantee monotonically improving realized averages or compensation after streaks.
section: The law of large numbers concerns concentration

name: Central limit theorem
quick: Standardized iid sums approach a normal distribution under finite positive variance.
definition: $(\bar X_n-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ converges in distribution to $N(0,1)$.
example: A binomial sum can have approximately normal standardized CDFs despite being discrete.
confusion: The CLT concerns sums or means, not normality of individual observations.
section: The central limit theorem describes standardized fluctuations

name: Continuity correction
quick: Adjust count thresholds by half a unit before a continuous approximation.
definition: Approximate $P(K\le k)$ using the continuous boundary $k+1/2$.
example: For $K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(100,1/2)$, $K\le55$ uses standardized threshold $1.1$.
confusion: Apply the half-unit correction on the count scale, not after standardization.
section: Approximate probabilities for means, sums, and proportions

name: Shared noise in an average
quick: A common random component does not disappear when readings are averaged.
example: A shared calibration error persists across repeated measurements.
confusion: More readings are not equivalent to more independent sources of information.
section: Check dependence, precision, and the limits of asymptotics

name: Markov inequality
quick: A mean controls a nonnegative upper tail.
example: Mean 12 gives $P(X\ge60)\le1/5$.
confusion: An upper bound is not the actual probability.
section: A mean can bound a nonnegative tail

name: Chebyshev inequality
quick: Variance bounds the chance of a large deviation.
example: Variance 9 gives a bound of $1/4$ at distance 6.
confusion: Normality is not required, but finite variance is.
section: Centering and squaring gives Chebyshev

name: Concentration guarantee
quick: A bound on the probability of estimation error.
definition: Under independence and common finite variance, $P(|\bar X-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$.
example: With $\sigma^2=4$, $\varepsilon=1/2$, $\delta=1/20$, $n=320$ suffices.
confusion: A sufficient sample size need not be necessary.
section: Guarantees for averages and sample sizes

name: Monte Carlo estimate
quick: An expectation approximated by a simulated sample average.
definition: For independent draws, $\hat I=n^{-1}\sum_i g(U_i)$ estimates $E[g(U)]$.
example: 37 successes in 100 simulated trials give $\hat p=0.37$.
confusion: Simulation error and model error are different.
section: Monte Carlo turns an expectation into an estimate

name: Union failure bound
quick: The probability of any failure is at most the sum of individual probabilities.
example: Eight failure bounds of $1/200$ give $1/25$.
confusion: Multiplying failure probabilities requires a different event and suitable independence.
section: From individual failures to algorithm guarantees

name: Estimator and estimate
quick: A random-data rule and its observed value.
definition: $\hat\Theta=T(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ is the estimator; $T(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ is the estimate.
example: Seven successes in twenty trials give the estimate $7/20$.
confusion: The estimate is not proof of the true parameter.
section: A parameter, an estimator, and an estimate

name: Estimator bias
quick: Repeated-sampling mean minus the target.
example: Mean 8 when the target is 10 gives bias $-2$.
confusion: Bias is not the realized error in one sample.
section: Bias and mean squared error

name: Estimator mean squared error
quick: Average squared estimation error.
example: Variance 4 and bias 1 give MSE 5.
confusion: An unbiased estimator can still have large MSE.
section: Bias and mean squared error

name: Consistent estimator
quick: Estimation error concentrates near zero as sample size increases.
example: An iid finite-variance sample mean is consistent.
confusion: Consistency is a limiting property, not exact finite-sample accuracy.
section: Consistency and the denominator in sample variance

name: Likelihood
quick: Observed-data mass or density viewed as a function of the parameter.
example: An ordered sequence with two successes and one failure has likelihood $p^2(1-p)$.
confusion: Likelihood is not a probability distribution over parameters.
section: Likelihood keeps the data fixed

name: Maximum likelihood estimate
quick: A permitted parameter maximizing observed-data likelihood.
example: For Bernoulli observations with 7 successes in 20 trials, $\hat p=7/20$.
confusion: A maximum-likelihood estimate does not quantify its own uncertainty.
section: Log-likelihood and elementary maximization

name: Confidence coverage
quick: How often a repeated-sampling interval procedure contains the fixed target.
definition: A level $1-\alpha$ procedure aims for $P_\theta(L(X)\le\theta\le U(X))=1-\alpha$, or an explicitly stated approximation.
example: An interval procedure covering the target in 950 of 1000 simulated repetitions has observed coverage 0.95.
confusion: Confidence is not the fraction of individual observations inside an interval for a mean.
section: Coverage belongs to a procedure

name: Margin of error
quick: The half-width in a symmetric interval construction.
definition: For a known-$\sigma$ mean interval, $m=z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$.
confusion: The margin is half the interval width, not its full width.
section: A mean interval with known population spread

name: Student t mean interval
quick: A mean interval accounting for an estimated standard deviation.
definition: $\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}S/\sqrt n$ under the stated normal sampling model.
example: Mean 20, $S=3$, $n=9$, and critical value 2.306 give $[17.694,22.306]$.
confusion: Using t does not remove independence or distributional assumptions.
section: Estimating spread leads to Student t

name: Wald proportion interval
quick: An introductory large-sample interval using a plug-in Bernoulli standard error.
example: 100 successes in 400 trials give $\hat p=1/4$.
confusion: Zero observed successes do not justify certainty that the population probability is zero.
section: Proportion intervals and boundary limitations

name: Precision planning
quick: Choosing a sample size for a stated margin under a specified model.
definition: For known $\sigma$, $n\ge(z\sigma/m)^2$ and the integer choice rounds upward.
confusion: A sampling margin does not include every source of error.
section: Planning precision and checking conclusions

name: Null and alternative hypotheses
quick: Population claims defining the reference and the departure of interest.
definition: An upper-sided mean test uses $H_0:\mu\le\mu_0$ and $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$.
example: A claim that mean latency exceeds 10 uses the alternative $\mu>10$.
confusion: Hypotheses concern a population parameter, not the observed sample mean.
section: State a claim about the population before examining evidence

name: p-value
quick: A tail probability for the chosen test statistic under the null model.
definition: For an upper-sided normal test, $p=1-\Phi(z_{\rm obs})$.
example: $\Phi(2)=0.97725$ gives upper-tail p-value 0.02275.
confusion: It is not the posterior probability that the null is true.
section: Tail probabilities under the null model

name: Significance level
quick: A preselected threshold controlling the test decision.
definition: Use the stated rule: reject when $p\le\alpha$.
example: A p-value of 0.03 rejects at 0.05 but not at 0.01.
confusion: Changing the threshold does not change the observed p-value.
section: Tail probabilities under the null model

name: One-sample standardized mean
quick: The observed mean departure divided by its standard error.
example: Mean 12, null 10, $\sigma=5$, $n=25$ give $Z=2$.
confusion: The reference distribution changes when the population spread is estimated.
section: Tests for a single population mean

name: Null standard error
quick: Sampling variability evaluated using the null parameter.
example: $p_0=1/2$, $n=100$ give $\operatorname{SE}_0=0.05$.
confusion: The plug-in confidence-interval standard error is a different calculation.
section: A proportion test uses the null standard error

name: Test power
quick: Rejection probability at a specified alternative.
example: Power 0.80 corresponds to Type II probability 0.20 at that alternative.
confusion: Power is not the probability that a rejection is correct.
section: Errors, power, and practical meaning

name: Type I and Type II errors
aliases: Type I and Type II errors
quick: False rejection and failure to reject a false null.
definition: Type I: reject a true $H_0$. Type II: fail to reject at a specified alternative.
example: Declaring an effect under a true no-effect null is Type I.
confusion: Failing to reject does not establish equivalence.
section: Errors, power, and practical meaning

name: Prior and posterior
quick: Parameter uncertainty before and after conditioning on data.
definition: Posterior mass or density is proportional to likelihood times prior, followed by normalization.
example: Equal prior masses at $1/4$ and $3/4$ become posterior masses $1/4$ and $3/4$ after one success.
confusion: The likelihood alone is not the posterior.
section: Model uncertainty about a parameter

name: Beta distribution
quick: A two-parameter family of densities on the unit interval.
example: Beta(2,2) has density $6p(1-p)$.
confusion: The same prior mean can accompany very different prior spreads.
section: Beta distributions on a probability parameter

name: Beta-binomial update
quick: Add successes and failures to the prior beta shapes.
example: Beta(2,3) with 3 successes in 4 trials becomes Beta(5,4).
confusion: Conditional independence and a common success probability are modeling assumptions.
section: Binomial data update both shape parameters

name: Posterior predictive probability
quick: A future-data probability averaged over posterior parameter uncertainty.
example: For Beta(2,2), one success has predictive probability $1/2$ and two successive successes have probability $3/10$.
confusion: Conditional independence given a parameter does not imply independence after averaging over it.
section: Predict future observations by averaging over uncertainty

name: Credible interval
quick: An interval containing a stated amount of posterior probability.
definition: A posterior credible interval satisfies $P(l\le\Theta\le u\mid D)=c$ for the stated probability $c$.
example: For posterior density $2p$, $[\sqrt{0.1},\sqrt{0.9}]$ has probability 0.8.
confusion: A posterior probability statement is different from repeated-sampling confidence coverage.
section: Credible intervals and sensitivity to assumptions

name: Regression residual
quick: Observed response minus fitted response.
example: If $y=8$ and $\widehat y=6$, the residual is $2$.
confusion: A residual is not the unobserved population error.
section: A fitted line and a population model

name: Centered predictor sum of squares
quick: $S_{xx}$ measures predictor spread.
definition: $S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2$; a positive value is needed to identify a slope.
confusion: It is a sum, not the sample variance divided by the sample size.
section: A fitted line and a population model

name: Residual standard error
quick: An estimate of the common error standard deviation.
definition: In simple regression with intercept and slope, $s=\sqrt{\operatorname{SSE}/(n-2)}$.
example: With $n=8$ and SSE $18$, $s=\sqrt3$.
confusion: Dividing by n gives the Gaussian maximum-likelihood variance estimate instead.
section: Why Gaussian likelihood gives least squares

name: Slope standard error
quick: Estimated sampling spread of the fitted slope.
example: With $s=2$ and $S_{xx}=100$, it is $1/5$.
confusion: It is not the slope, residual variance, or standard deviation of the predictors.
section: Uncertainty in a coefficient

name: Prediction interval
quick: An interval for a future individual response.
definition: For a new response at $x_0$, use $\widehat y_0\pm t^*s\sqrt{1+1/n+(x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}}$.
example: Its squared standard error exceeds that for the mean by $s^2$.
confusion: A confidence interval for the mean response omits individual noise and is narrower when s is positive.
section: Predicting a mean and predicting one new observation

name: Leverage
quick: Potential influence associated with unusual predictor values.
definition: Predictor values far from $\bar x$ can give an observation substantial influence on the fitted line.
example: One point far to the right can rotate a fitted line while retaining a small residual.
confusion: High leverage and a large residual are different properties.
section: Assumptions, diagnostics, and the limits of a slope

name: Empirical distribution
quick: Equal probability on each observed row.
definition: Each of $n$ recorded observations has weight $1/n$; equal values accumulate their weights.
example: For $2,2,5$, the empirical probability of $2$ is $2/3$.
confusion: It describes a sample-based distribution, not certainty about the population probabilities.
section: The empirical distribution and resampling units

name: Bootstrap sample
quick: A same-size sample drawn with replacement from observed data.
definition: For independent rows, select $n$ row indices independently and uniformly from $1,\ldots,n$.
example: From three rows, indices $(2,2,1)$ form a valid bootstrap sample.
confusion: Without replacement at the same size only rearranges the original sample.
section: The empirical distribution and resampling units

name: Bootstrap standard error
quick: Estimated spread of a statistic over resampled datasets.
definition: Use the sample standard deviation of independently simulated bootstrap estimates, with denominator $B-1$.
example: Replicates $1,2,3$ have sample standard deviation $1$.
confusion: More bootstrap replicates improve simulation precision; they do not create more original observations.
section: Bootstrap uncertainty versus more simulation

name: Validation data
quick: Held-out data used to choose models or settings.
definition: Validation results guide selection; a final test evaluates the selected procedure without guiding it.
example: Choose polynomial degree by validation MSE, then report performance on a reserved test set.
confusion: Repeatedly selecting against the test set turns it into validation data.
section: Training, validation, and a final test

name: Data leakage
quick: Evaluation information influencing model construction.
definition: Leakage includes preprocessing, feature selection, and tuning using information intended to be held out.
example: Computing a centering mean using test observations leaks their feature information.
confusion: A label need not be copied directly into training for leakage to occur.
section: Training, validation, and a final test

name: Classification precision
quick: Fraction of predicted positives that are actual positives.
example: Twelve correct positives among twenty positive predictions give precision $3/5$.
confusion: Recall conditions on actual positives instead.
section: Reading a confusion matrix

name: Classification recall
quick: Fraction of actual positives identified as positive.
example: Twelve detected positives out of sixteen actual positives give recall $3/4$.
confusion: High accuracy on an imbalanced sample does not ensure high recall.
section: Reading a confusion matrix

name: Expected prediction loss
quick: Average loss under the population where predictions will be used.
definition: For finite cases, risk is $\sum_i p_i\,\ell_i$; held-out average loss estimates it under a representative design.
example: Losses $1,5$ with probabilities $3/4,1/4$ give risk $2$.
confusion: Training loss, selected validation loss, and future population loss have different roles.
section: Matching assessment to the decision
